source_refs.note: Post-Transcriptional Modifications: a main subheading of The Phases of Transcription and mRNA Processing, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 135-136.

blocks.text: As the prokaryotes have no nucleus and transcription happens in cytoplasm, their new mRNA does not need to travel anywhere to start translation. On the other hand, in eukaryotic cells the new mRNA has to travel from nucleus to cytoplasm. For this journey, the new mRNA undergoes the following modifications.

1- Addition of 5′ Cap: The first nucleotide (at the 5′ end of mRNA) is A or G. At the terminal 5′ end of A or G a methylated GTP is attached. This bond is formed between 5′end of terminal A or G and 5′end of GTP. This structure is called a 5′ cap. It protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases during its journey.
2- Addition of 3′ Poly-A tail: At the 3′end of mRNA, a small chain of about 250 A nucleotides is added. It is called 3′ poly-A tail. It protects the mRNA transcript from degradation by nucleases.

blocks.alt: Template DNA 3' to 5' with a promoter and four exons separated by three introns; transcription gives the immature mRNA 5' to 3' with the same exons and introns; addition of a 5' cap (GTP) and a 3' poly-A tail (AAAA); mRNA splicing removes the introns and gives the mature mRNA: 5' cap, protein-coding sequence, 3' poly-A tail, ready to move to cytoplasm. A bracket marks the steps after transcription as post-transcriptional modifications.

blocks.text: 3- Splicing: The new mRNA is immature because it contains introns (regions of DNA or mRNA that do not code for proteins) and exons (regions of DNA or mRNA which are "expressed" or translated into a protein). mRNA splicing is the process by which introns are removed from the immature mRNA. After splicing, the remaining exons are joined. So, the mature RNA consists of coding segments (gene) only.
